hook.text: Drowsy driving causes about 100,000 crashes a year in the US alone.

buildup.text: A tired driver drifts across the lane line without correcting because their brain is asleep.

discovery.text: Lane-keeping systems use cameras to read road markings and steer the car back if it drifts.

twist.text: Early versions only beeped—modern ones actually turn the steering wheel to nudge you back.

climax.text: Cars with lane-keeping assist show clear reductions in sideswipe and head-on collisions.

punchline.text: The car steers you back while you're still waking up.

quiz.question: What does modern lane-keeping assist do when you drift?
options: Gently steers the car back into the lane

details.summary: Lane keeping assist uses cameras to track road markings and gently steers or vibrates the wheel to keep the vehicle centered in its lane, counteracting drowsy or distracted drifting.
details.whyItMatters: Lane departure is a leading cause of head-on collisions and run-off-road crashes. Lane keeping assist provides a critical safety net for tired or inattentive drivers on highways.
takeaways: Cameras identify lane markings and track vehicle position
The system applies corrective steering or haptic alerts
It reduces unintentional lane departure accidents markedly

faq.question: Does lane keeping assist work on roads without clear markings?
faq.answer: Most systems require visible lane markings to function. On rural roads, construction zones, or in heavy snow where lines are obscured, the system may disengage or perform poorly.

faq.question: Is lane keeping assist the same as automatic lane centering?
faq.answer: Lane keeping assist intervenes only when you drift near a lane edge, while lane centering continuously steers to keep the car in the middle. Lane centering is a more advanced feature.
